chunks: Mousebites on PCB panels. The question: What are mousebites?
A mousebite is a row of small drilled holes through a narrow tab that holds a board inside its panel.
The holes weaken the tab on purpose, so it snaps along a known line when you bend it. Mousebites are not a defect.
They are how boards cut out by a milling bit (routed boards) come out of a panel cleanly.
Think of a sheet of paper with a perforated tear line. You do not tear it wherever it happens to give. It rips along the dotted holes.
A mousebite tab works the same way: the tab would resist breaking if solid, but with holes drilled through it, the break follows the row of holes.
The name comes from the little scalloped bumps left on the board edge, which look like bites. Unlike paper, a board has parts on it that can be damaged by the bending.
A routed outline with one tab bridging the board to the panel. The perforation line (red holes) sits on the board's edge, so the break happens flush with the outline.
The dashed lines show the routed slot on each side of the tab.
Tab: a narrow bridge of board material that keeps a routed-out board attached to the panel. Perforation: the row of small holes drilled through the tab.
Stub: the small rough bump left on the board edge after the tab breaks. Non-plated hole: a hole with no copper lining, so snapping it leaves no copper burrs.
Keep-out: an area around the tab where copper and parts are not allowed. Panel: the frame of boards built together.
Take a tab 3 mm wide, with 0. 5 mm holes spaced 0. 8 mm center to center. Four holes fit across the tab. Between neighboring holes only a thin strip of 0. 8 - 0. 5 = 0.
3 mm of board is left. Those thin strips are all that hold the board, so a modest bend breaks them in a straight line. That is the whole idea.
"Mousebites are rows of small, non-plated drilled holes through the narrow tabs that hold a routed board in a panel.
They perforate the tab so it snaps cleanly where I want it when I break the board out. They're used for odd shapes where V-score can't work.
The trade-off is a small stub on the edge, so I keep parts and copper clear of the tabs and make sure the stub doesn't interfere with the enclosure."
